quarterly_data.signal: Q2 FY2026 CALL (December quarter) - HEADLINE: CFO Amy Hood: 'revenue was $81.3 billion, up 17% in constant currency'; operating income up 21% in constant currency; earnings per share $4.14 (up 24% in constant currency when adjusted for the impact of the OpenAI investment); company gross margin 68% and operating margin 47%. CEO Satya Nadella: 'the Microsoft Cloud surpassed $50 billion in revenue for the first time, up 26% year over year' - Microsoft Cloud revenue was $51.5 billion at a 67% gross margin. Intelligent Cloud revenue was $32.9 billion, up 29% in constant currency; 'Azure and other cloud services, revenue grew 39% in constant currency, slightly ahead of expectations with ongoing efficiency gains across our fungible fleet enabling us to reallocate some capacity to Azure that was monetized in the quarter.' On-premises server revenue grew 21% in constant currency, helped by the SQL Server 2025 launch and 'higher transactional purchasing ahead of memory price increases.' GAAP other income and expense was $10 billion, driven by a gain tied to OpenAI's recapitalization (Microsoft still uses the equity method and now records its share of the change in OpenAI's net assets).
quarterly_data.figure: revenue $81.3 billion (up 17% cc); Microsoft Cloud $51.5 billion (26%); Intelligent Cloud $32.9 billion (29% cc); Azure and other cloud services 39% cc; EPS $4.14

quarterly_data.signal: CALL - CAPEX AND SUPPLY: capital expenditures were $37.5 billion in the quarter, and 'roughly two-thirds of our CapEx, was on short-lived assets, primarily GPUs and CPUs'; the remaining spend went to long-lived assets 'that will support monetization for the next fifteen years and beyond.' Finance leases were $6.7 billion ('primarily for large data center sites'), cash paid for PP and E was $29.9 billion, and free cash flow fell sequentially to $5.9 billion on higher cash capex. Hood: 'Our customer demand continues to exceed our supply,' so incoming supply has to be balanced across Azure demand, first-party AI usage (Microsoft 365 Copilot, GitHub Copilot), larger allocations to R and D teams, and replacement of end-of-life server and networking equipment. Q3 FY2026 outlook: capex expected to DECREASE sequentially 'due to a normal variability from cloud infrastructure build-outs and the timing of delivery of finance leases', with the short-lived-asset mix staying similar to Q2 while Microsoft works to close the gap between demand and supply. Hood added that much of the GPU capacity being bought is 'already contracted for most of their useful life' - GPU contracts, 'including for some of our largest customers', are 'sold for the entire useful life of the GPU'.
quarterly_data.figure: capex $37.5 billion (roughly two-thirds short-lived GPUs and CPUs); finance leases $6.7 billion; cash paid for PP and E $29.9 billion; Q3 capex to decrease sequentially

quarterly_data.signal: CALL - BACKLOG: commercial remaining performance obligation (reported net of reserves) increased to $625 billion with a weighted average duration of approximately two and a half years (Hood: extended 'from around two years to two and a half', driven by longer-duration Azure contracts); roughly 25% will be recognized in revenue in the next twelve months (that portion up 39% year over year) and the portion beyond twelve months increased 56%. 'Approximately 45% of our commercial RPO balance is from OpenAI'; the other 55%, 'roughly $350 billion', spans a broad set of customers, solutions, industries and geographies and grew 28% - Hood: 'larger than most peers. More diversified than most peers.' Commercial bookings increased 23% in constant currency, driven by the large multiyear Azure commitment from OpenAI and the previously announced Anthropic commitment from November; Hood warned the OpenAI contract signed in Q2 'will result in some quarterly volatility in both bookings and RPO growth rates going forward.' Nadella said software lets Microsoft keep running the latest models on an aging fleet, and Hood said that where capacity is sold for its entire life 'the margins actually improved with time.'
quarterly_data.figure: commercial RPO $625 billion; approximately 45% from OpenAI; remaining 55% (roughly $350 billion) grew 28%; commercial bookings up 23% cc

quarterly_data.signal: DELL RUNS 'FOUR MOVING TO FIVE' DIFFERENT SOURCES OF TOKENS - THE TOKEN-ECONOMICS CASE FOR HYBRID/ON-PREM INFRASTRUCTURE. Global CTO and Chief AI Officer John Roese said the first principle of token economics in the agentic era 'is you have got to have a diverse source of intelligence... sources that range from different compliance levels, different capabilities, but also different economic strata. At Dell Technologies, I have four moving to five different fundamental sources of tokens. They have very different economics. I run open models on-prem in my data centers. I run frontier models in my data centers. I run frontier models in VPCs I control. I use APIs. I now run models on devices using things like personal agent frameworks.' He grounded it in unit economics: an agent that helps the CEO decide in real time can be worth '$100,000 a month to run', while an agent cleaning CRM records where 'each CRM record it cleans up has an economic value of $0.50' needs an environment where 'it does not cost $12 in tokens to do a $0.50 task'. A customer on 'a single provider with a single set of models over a single economic model... fundamentally wouldn't be able to do the CRM agent because it's just not affordable in that model' - the demand argument for on-prem and VPC inference capacity rather than API-only consumption.
quarterly_data.figure: four moving to five fundamental sources of tokens (on-prem open, on-prem frontier, VPC frontier, API, on-device); $100,000 a month agent vs a $0.50 CRM record that must not cost $12 in tokens

Customers say server demand is solid (the refresh cycle is not over, plus agentic AI and inference applications) but that they will be constrained by supply, and lead times continue to lengthen on the supply side: 'in 2026, the demand is solid. But we're going to be more constrained by supply than we're going to be by demand.' Agentic AI is catalyzing traditional CPU-based server demand and the need for more DIMMs per system; the average number of DIMMs per channel keeps growing but is hard to quantify, and the memory market overall is expected to be constrained.

Rambus targets companies developing their own accelerators, inference chips and processors with a laser-focused portfolio (PCIe, CXL, HBM, GDDR and security IP) that can support a large number of customers.
